title: Describing a Place
subtitle: Four rooms, and what changes when you write down what you can hear and smell instead of what you can see.
description: A B2 reading and listening text with four short descriptive scenes — a kitchen, a campsite, a training room and a shopping centre — used to teach sensory vocabulary and the difference between describing and cataloguing.
passage: Most people describing a place list what they can see, and the result is flat. What makes a written place feel real is usually a sound, a smell, or something physical you would notice with your eyes shut. Here are four, each built around a different sense.

The coffee has been on long enough for the smell to have reached the stairs. Bacon is going in a pan, which is the loudest thing in the room, and under it there is the slower sound of oatmeal moving in a pot. Sunlight comes through thin curtains and lands on the counter. Somebody is cutting fruit, and the knife against the board is the rhythm the rest of it sits on — strawberries, then something harder, a kiwi maybe, which makes a different sound. The coffee machine gives a last splutter and stops. A cup is filled. There is the noise of plates and two people talking, and the specific comfort of a room where breakfast is nearly ready and nobody has to be anywhere for another hour.

Pine, first, and then woodsmoke. The fire has got past the crackling stage and settled into the occasional pop. Tents stand in a loose circle, dulled to brown and green in the failing light. There is a stream somewhere close enough to hear and not close enough to see. A cast-iron pan is on a portable stove and whatever is in it has started to catch slightly at the edges, which is not a problem. People are on folding chairs with their faces lit from below, and the conversation has reached the stage where nobody is trying to be interesting. Later somebody gets a guitar out, and later than that the tents glow from the inside as lanterns go on, and the sky over the clearing turns out to have considerably more stars in it than anybody remembered.

The sound in a jiu-jitsu room is bodies hitting a mat, which is duller and heavier than people expect. Bare feet shuffle and slap. The mats smell of rubber and of the disinfectant used on them that morning. Pairs circle each other, and the circling is the longest part; the technique, when it comes, takes about a second and a half. The instructor moves between them correcting grips with two fingers. Everybody's breathing has synchronised without anybody deciding to, and the only voices are short — a name, a laugh, somebody tapping out and both of them resetting. It looks like fighting and behaves like a very physical argument conducted in a language both people have agreed to speak.

Then the opposite of all three. The shopping centre after work is noise with no pattern in it: escalators, tills, several hundred conversations, and a track playing somewhere that nobody is listening to. The air is warm and carries coffee, perfume and the particular smell of new clothes. Everybody is walking slightly faster than is comfortable and apologising without looking up. The queue at the checkout is the one place the pace breaks, and people standing in it look at each other for the first time — somebody's child asleep against their shoulder, somebody holding a single item and visibly regretting the whole trip. Ten minutes later you are outside with a bag in each hand, and the quiet of the car park is startling.

Notice what the four have in common. Almost nothing is described by colour. What is doing the work is sound — the knife, the fire, the mat, the escalators — and smell, which is the sense writers use least and readers trust most. Notice also that each one contains a small human observation that could not have been guessed from the setting: nobody having to be anywhere for an hour, nobody trying to be interesting, the argument conducted in an agreed language, the man regretting the trip. That is the difference between describing a place and listing its contents.

vocabulary.definition: dull and lifeless, said of writing
to be cooking noisily
the wooden or plastic surface you cut food on

made less bright

exercises.title: Reading for Technique
exercises.instructions: This text describes four places and then explains what it was doing. Read for both.

items.prompt: Why does the writer say most descriptions come out flat?
options: They list what can be seen, and leave out sound and smell
items.explanation: “Something physical you would notice with your eyes shut” is the test offered instead.

items.prompt: In the kitchen, what does the writer call “the rhythm the rest of it sits on”?
options: The knife against the cutting board
items.explanation: And the detail that a kiwi makes a different sound from a strawberry is what makes it convincing.

items.prompt: What does “the fire has got past the crackling stage” tell you?
options: The fire has been burning for some time
The fire is about to go out
items.explanation: Crackling is what a new fire does; an established one settles to the occasional pop.

items.prompt: What does the writer say about the food catching in the pan?
items.explanation: A small piece of tolerance that tells you what kind of evening it is.

items.prompt: What surprises people about the sound in the training room?
options: That bodies hitting a mat sound duller and heavier than expected
items.explanation: The writer corrects an expectation the reader probably brought from films.

items.prompt: How does the writer describe what jiu-jitsu actually resembles?
options: A physical argument conducted in a language both people have agreed to speak
items.explanation: It “looks like fighting” and behaves like something else — the agreement is what separates them.

items.prompt: Where does the pace break in the shopping centre?
options: In the queue at the checkout
items.explanation: And that is where people look at each other “for the first time”.

items.prompt: Which sense does the writer say is used least and trusted most?
items.explanation: Stated in the closing paragraph, alongside the observation that almost nothing in the four scenes is described by colour.

items.prompt: What does the writer say each scene contains besides sensory detail?
options: A small human observation that could not be guessed from the setting
items.explanation: Nobody having to be anywhere, nobody trying to be interesting, the agreed language, the man regretting the trip.

items.prompt: What is “the difference between describing a place and listing its contents”?
options: The human observation, and the use of senses other than sight
items.explanation: Which is the whole argument the four scenes were assembled to demonstrate.

exercises.title: Sensory Vocabulary
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with the word that carries the sound, smell or texture.

items.prompt: The fire had stopped ___ and settled to the occasional pop.
items.explanation: To crackle is to make small sharp popping sounds — what a new fire does.

items.prompt: The stew had begun to ___ at the edges of the pan.
items.explanation: To catch is to start burning slightly on the bottom — a cooking sense of a very common verb.

items.prompt: He ___ across the mat without lifting his feet.
items.explanation: To shuffle is to move your feet without lifting them properly.

items.prompt: She ___ ___ and they both ___ and started again.
items.explanation: To tap out is to signal surrender in grappling; to reset is to return to the start.

items.prompt: The tents were ___ to brown and green in the ___ light.
items.explanation: Dulled means made less bright; failing light is the last of the daylight as it goes.

items.prompt: After all that noise, the quiet outside was ___.
items.explanation: Startling means surprising enough to make you stop — the last word of the shopping-centre scene.

exercises.title: True or False?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether each statement matches the text.

items.statement: The four scenes rely mainly on colour.
items.explanation: False — “almost nothing is described by colour”. Sound and smell do the work.

items.statement: The stream at the campsite is visible.
items.explanation: False — “close enough to hear and not close enough to see”.

items.statement: In jiu-jitsu, the circling takes longer than the technique.
items.explanation: True — the circling is “the longest part” and the technique takes about a second and a half.

items.statement: People in the shopping centre look at each other as they walk.
items.explanation: False — they apologise “without looking up”. They look at each other only in the queue.

items.statement: The writer says smell is the sense writers use most.
items.explanation: False — the least used, and the most trusted by readers.

discussion: Describe the room you are in now in five sentences, without naming a single colour.
“The sense writers use least and readers trust most.” Why do you think smell works that way?
Each scene has one observation that could not be guessed from the setting. Find them, and say which is the best.
Which of the four places would you most want to be in right now, and what detail decided it?
Write about 200 words describing a place you know well. Use at least three sounds, one smell, and one small observation about the people in it.
